stories.headline: Kulgam quake puts Kashmir’s seismic risk in focus
stories.title: Kulgam quake puts Kashmir’s seismic risk in focus
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 1: A 3.6-magnitude earthquake in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district has brought renewed attention to the seismic risks facing the valley, where active faults and complex geological structures make large areas vulnerable to earthquakes. Earth scientists say detailed mapping of local hazards, safer construction and preparedness are essential to limit the damage from future earthquakes. The earthquake struck DamhalHanjipora at 1:00:46 am on Friday at a depth of 10 km, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS). Its epicentre was recorded at latitude 33.628° N and longitude 74.922° E. Prof Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, eminent earth scientist and Vice Chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology (IUST), said the tremor was a reminder of Kashmir’s active tectonic setting. “Although an earthquake of this magnitude is minor, its shallow depth made the tremors perceptible in nearby areas,” Romshoo said. “Such earthquakes are not unusual in the seismically active Kashmir Himalaya and should be interpreted as part of the region’s larger seismicity.” He said earthquakes could not be predicted in terms of their timing, location or magnitude. “Preparedness, establishing a culture of disaster preparedness and risk-reduction measures are our most effective safeguards against future earthquake disasters,” Prof Ramshoo said. Riyaz Ahmad Mir, a scientist at the National Institute of Hydrology’s Western Himalayan Regional Centre (WHRC), Jammu, said several regional and local faults, thrusts and other active tectonic structures traverse Kashmir. “DH Pora, Kulgam, is no exception. The area is influenced by tectonic structures such as the Balapur Fault and Jhelum Fault. Furthermore, the southwestern PirPanjal is considered tectonically active, adding to the regional seismic hazard,” Mir said. The Balapur Fault is a reverse or thrust fault, where pressure pushes one block of the Earth’s crust over another. The Jhelum Fault is a strike-slip fault, along which blocks of the crust move horizontally past each other. Mir said the risk at a particular location depends on its proximity to faults, geological conditions, site characteristics and the vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure. Much of Kashmir falls in Seismic Zone V, the highest earthquake hazard category under India’s current classification. Parts of the Chenab Valley - Doda, Ramban and Kishtwar districts in the Jammu region— also fall in Zone V, while areas including the PirPanjal region - Rajouri and Poonch -are classified under Zone IV. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) ’IS 1893:2016 divides the country into four seismic zones; II, III, IV, and V. Zone IV denotes high seismic hazard, while Zone V denotes very high hazard. Zone VI was proposed in the revised seismic zonation in 2025 to represent the exceptionally high earthquake hazard of the Himalayan region but was subsequently withdrawn. Mir said the Himalaya was a continuous, tectonically active mountain belt largely governed by the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT), but earthquake hazard varied across the range. “Seismic zoning divides the region based on differences in expected ground shaking, earthquake potential, tectonic segmentation, local fault systems, geological conditions and historical seismicity,” he said. Mir said broad regional classifications could overlook local differences in risk, even within the same seismic zone. “The presence of a common active tectonic system does not imply identical seismic hazard everywhere. However, broad regional zoning may oversimplify local variations,” he said. He called for detailed seismic microzonation and active fault mapping to assess earthquake risk across the Himalaya. The experts also called for strict enforcement of earthquake-resistant building codes, assessment of vulnerable structures and regular safety drills in schools and public institutions.

stories.headline: FPI buying returns to Dalal Street as global investors rethink AI bets
stories.title: FPI buying returns to Dalal Street as global investors rethink AI bets
stories.summary: Mumbai: After aggressively selling in September and the first half of October, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have turned net buyers of Indian equities, investing nearly $1.2 billion over the past 10 trading sessions. Concerns over the outlook for the AI trade could have prompted some overseas investors to shift allocations to beaten-down Indian equities, which have lagged behind various regional peers recently in the absence of a dominant AI industry. The recent purchases, however, may be positional flows looking for avenues that are less impacted by the AI sell-off rather than a fresh bullish call on India by global investors."Indian large-cap stocks, particularly banks and IT companies, are being viewed as an anti-AI trade, attracting model-driven flows rather than a broad-based return of long-only foreign investors, said Ritesh Jain, founder of Pinetree Macro.135441127Between October 16 and October 30, FPIs made net purchases of nearly $1.2 billion in the secondary market, according to NSDL data. On October 30, they bought equities worth ₹3,600 crore, according to provisional NSE data. In the primary market, they were buyers worth $600 million, with Jio Telecom's ₹30,188 crore IPO expected to have cornered a large chunk of these flows."There is a shift in global investment flows because of signs of a deflation in the artificial intelligence (AI) trade," said Jain. "When the AI trade is doing well, money moves from the rest of the world into the US as investors buy dollars to invest in US AI stocks. When they sell these stocks, they also move out of the US dollar."Read more: Nifty IT’s 18% rally may mark a durable leadership cycle; 35,000 next: LKP's Vatsal BhuvaIndian markets delivered a mixed performance in October. The Sensex and Nifty gained 1.9% and 2.7%, respectively, while the BSE Midcap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 fell 4% and 6.3%. The Nifty IT index surged 17%.Overseas markets, meanwhile, saw sharp corrections, with the Nasdaq and Japan's Nikkei falling 5% each, Hong Kong's Hang Seng declining 5.5%, Shenzhen dropping 13.7%, and Taiwan and South Korea's Kospi falling 8% and 14%, respectively.Fund managers are seeing selective opportunities in India after the recent underperformance, said strategists. "A small portion of the inflows reflected selective foreign investors returning to India on a bottom-up basis, attracted by improving growth prospects and opportunities in certain technology sectors," said Gautam Chhaochharia, head of global markets, India, at UBS.Read more: Bonus issues, stock splits, dividends: Infosys, Asian Paints among over 40 stocks turning ex-date this weekThe recent buying follows a prolonged period of foreign outflows. Between January 1 and October 15, they sold equities worth over $32.7 billion amid the US-Iran war, rising crude oil prices, hardening bond yields, currency depreciation, earnings uncertainty and inflation. They had also sold equities worth over $18.8 billion in 2025.Though overseas investors bought nearly $6.15 billion in Indian equities between mid-June and August, they pulled out $8.6 billion in September and the first half of October as a spike in global oil prices and hardening of US bond yields heightened risk-off sentiment."The recent pressure on Indian markets had been driven more by global factors, including the strength of the AI trade and higher energy prices, than by domestic fundamentals," said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for Middle East and Asia-Pacific at BlackRock Investment Institute.BlackRock remains strategically overweight on India and is closely monitoring the recent pace of foreign inflows. "We continue to closely watch the encouraging recent pace of inflows and remain strategically overweight India," he said.

stories.headline: Mubarak Gul’s Exclusion
stories.title: Mubarak Gul’s Exclusion
stories.summary: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s recent cabinet expansion, with the induction of four new ministers, has triggered resentment within the National Conference (NC). After nearly two years of waiting, the long-awaited cabinet expansion has left many senior party leaders disappointed, raising questions about the leadership’s approach towards recognising its senior leaders and understanding regional aspirations. When Omar Abdullah selected his cabinet in 2024, he inducted only two Ministers from Kashmir Sakina Yatoo and Javed Ahmad Dar and gave more representation to Jammu by getting three MLAs appointed as Cabinet Ministers (Surinder Chowdhary, Satish Sharma and Javed Rana). By appointing a Hindu from Jammu as Deputy CM & an independent MLA from Jammu as cabinet Minister Omar Abdullah had taken great decision then. I wish he had appointed few more Ministers then only and closed this chapter. The fresh cabinet expansion was expected to address political aspirations across Jammu and Kashmir. Instead, it has exposed the discontent within the ruling party and different regions. Senior NC leader and seven-time MLA Mubarak Gul has expressed disappointment over his exclusion from the Council of Ministers. Another senior leader, Abdul Majid Larmi, a three-time MLA, was visibly emotional while speaking to the media. MLA from Gurez and former Deputy Speaker Nazir Ahmad Khan Gurezi reportedly stayed away from the swearing-in ceremony in protest against his exclusion. The resentment was not confined to individual leaders as many MLAs from the Pir Panjal region of Rajouri and Poonch reportedly met following the cabinet expansion, expressing concern over what they perceived as inadequate representation for their region and the Pahari community. Thanamandi MLA Muzaffar Iqbal Khan openly voiced these concerns. These developments suggest that the cabinet expansion, rather than consolidating the party, has created new political challenges for the National Conference leadership. A veteran leader denied his due? As per my personal assessment, Mubarak Gul’s exclusion from the Council of Ministers is particularly difficult to justify politically. Gul first won the Eidgah Assembly constituency in 1983 and has since built a long political career, winning seven Assembly elections, including the 2024 election. His association with the National Conference goes back to mid 1970s. Before entering electoral politics, he headed the Jammu and Kashmir Youth Federation, which later became part of the Youth National Conference. Despite his long service to the party and repeated electoral victories, Gul has never been given a cabinet portfolio by his own party. He did serve as Speaker of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly from 2013 to 2015, an important constitutional position. Nevertheless, the question remains: why has a leader with such a long electoral record and organisational experience never been accommodated in the Council of Ministers? The manner in which the party has responded to Gul’s disappointment is also reminiscent of an earlier episode in his political career. In 1987, when Gul was serving as president of the Youth National Conference, he was denied the party mandate from Eidgah. According to the political account of that period, Dr Farooq Abdullah subsequently took him to the Nawai Subah party office and appointed him Provincial President to address his grievances. History appears to have repeated itself. Following the recent cabinet expansion, Gul was again taken to the National Conference headquarters at Nawai Subah, where Dr Farooq Abdullah and senior party leaders welcomed him with garlands. An announcement was subsequently made appointing him General Secretary of the party. Later the order was retracted. Is this how National Conference appoints its office bearers? This means all the elections held for different party posts in the past were just a mockery? While an organisational position is important, it cannot automatically substitute for the responsibility and authority associated with a cabinet portfolio. After nearly five decades of association with the party, Gul’s exclusion raises legitimate questions about how the NC rewards its veteran leaders. Eidgah side-lined? Mubarak Gul’s exclusion also brings into focus a wider question concerning the political representation and development of Eidgah constituency in Srinagar. To my knowledge, no MLA representing Eidgah from 1947 till date has been appointed a minister, despite Gul’s repeated electoral victories. This deserves closer examination, particularly when representatives from other constituencies in Srinagar and from relatively remote areas of Jammu and Kashmir have held ministerial positions or other significant responsibilities in different governments. The issue is not merely about awarding a position to an individual politician. It is also about whether the people of a constituency receive adequate political attention and effective representation within the government. Eidgah has its own pressing civic and developmental concerns. The Achan garbage dumping site, in particular, remains an important issue affecting residents and the surrounding environment. Questions relating to waste management, public health, infrastructure and basic civic amenities require sustained political attention. I believe that the perceived political marginalisation of Eidgah deserves serious scrutiny. While the absence of a minister from a constituency does not, by itself, establish the cause of its developmental shortcomings, ensuring a stronger voice for the constituency in government could help its concerns receive greater attention. The National Conference leadership should explain how it intends to address these longstanding grievances. Pir Panjal and the question of regional representation The resentment expressed by Muzaffar Iqbal Khan highlights another important dimension of the cabinet expansion: the representation of the Pir Panjal region and the Pahari community. Rajouri and Poonch occupy a strategically and politically significant position in Jammu and Kashmir. Their people have distinct developmental priorities, including connectivity, healthcare, education, employment and access to public services. The region also has a diverse social composition, making balanced political representation particularly important. The disappointment expressed by MLAs from the region indicates that some elected representatives believe their constituencies have not received adequate consideration in the formation of the new Council of Ministers. The Pahari community has several elected representatives, including leaders such as Dr Sajad Shafi , Javed Mirchal, Javed Hassan Beigh, Ajaz Jan and Muzaffar Iqbal Khan. The precise number of MLAs belonging to the community and their respective constituencies should be established before drawing definitive conclusions about its representation. In my assessment, the leadership should have considered inducting a minister from the Pahari community, particularly from Rajouri or Poonch, if the objective was to ensure a more equitable regional balance. If the leadership considered retaining Shamima Firdous in the Council of Ministers, it could also have examined alternative arrangements for accommodating other regional aspirations. Similarly, senior party leaders who were not inducted into the government could have been considered for important organisational responsibilities. These are political choices, and reasonable people may disagree about the best combination of ministers. However, a transparent explanation of the criteria used to select ministers would have helped address the resentment now visible within the party. Abdul Majid Larmi, Dr Veeri The emotional reaction of Abdul Majid Larmi is another indication of the discontent generated by the cabinet expansion. Larmi stated that he had been among the prospective candidates for ministerial induction and expressed dissatisfaction with the leadership’s decision concerning South Kashmir’s representation. He also questioned the induction of Pahalgam MLA Altaf Kaloo, whom he considered junior to himself. While seniority alone cannot be the deciding criterion for ministerial appointments, the disappointment of a three-time MLA deserves to be addressed through meaningful engagement rather than mere symbolic gestures. Promising NC leaders like Dr Bashir Veeri have also been side-lined by the party, especially the CM who rebuked him on the floor of the house when he raised an issue related to the hike in electricity bills? How can a CM behave like this with his MLAs? Mir Saifullah deserved better consideration Apart from the selection of cabinet ministers, the allocation of portfolios also warrants closer examination. In my opinion, Mir Saifullah should have been considered for the Jal Shakti portfolio, which covers important responsibilities relating to drinking water supply and irrigation, including flood-control functions within the relevant administrative framework. Water supply, irrigation and flood management are critical sectors in Jammu and Kashmir especially for the border district of Kupwara. The success of this cabinet will be judged not by the ceremony of its formation, but by its ability to deliver on the ground. Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat is an Acumen Fellow. opening: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s recent cabinet expansion, with the induction of four new ministers, has triggered resentment within the National Conference (NC).

After nearly two years of waiting, the long-awaited cabinet expansion has left many senior party leaders disappointed, raising questions about the leadership’s approach towards recognising its senior leaders and understanding regional aspirations.
body: When Omar Abdullah selected his cabinet in 2024, he inducted only two Ministers from Kashmir Sakina Yatoo and Javed Ahmad Dar and gave more representation to Jammu by getting three MLAs appointed as Cabinet Ministers (Surinder Chowdhary, Satish Sharma and Javed Rana).
By appointing a Hindu from Jammu as Deputy CM & an independent MLA from Jammu as cabinet Minister Omar Abdullah had taken great decision then.
I wish he had appointed few more Ministers then only and closed this chapter.
Instead, it has exposed the discontent within the ruling party and different regions.
Senior NC leader and seven-time MLA Mubarak Gul has expressed disappointment over his exclusion from the Council of Ministers.
Another senior leader, Abdul Majid Larmi, a three-time MLA, was visibly emotional while speaking to the media.
MLA from Gurez and former Deputy Speaker Nazir Ahmad Khan Gurezi reportedly stayed away from the swearing-in ceremony in protest against his exclusion.

The resentment was not confined to individual leaders as many MLAs from the Pir Panjal region of Rajouri and Poonch reportedly met following the cabinet expansion, expressing concern over what they perceived as inadequate representation for their region and the Pahari community.
Thanamandi MLA Muzaffar Iqbal Khan openly voiced these concerns.
These developments suggest that the cabinet expansion, rather than consolidating the party, has created new political challenges for the National Conference leadership.
A veteran leader denied his due?
As per my personal assessment, Mubarak Gul’s exclusion from the Council of Ministers is particularly difficult to justify politically.
Gul first won the Eidgah Assembly constituency in 1983 and has since built a long political career, winning seven Assembly elections, including the 2024 election.
His association with the National Conference goes back to mid 1970s.
Before entering electoral politics, he headed the Jammu and Kashmir Youth Federation, which later became part of the Youth National Conference.
Despite his long service to the party and repeated electoral victories, Gul has never been given a cabinet portfolio by his own party.
He did serve as Speaker of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly from 2013 to 2015, an important constitutional position.
Nevertheless, the question remains: why has a leader with such a long electoral record and organisational experience never been accommodated in the Council of Ministers?
The manner in which the party has responded to Gul’s disappointment is also reminiscent of an earlier episode in his political career.
In 1987, when Gul was serving as president of the Youth National Conference, he was denied the party mandate from Eidgah.
According to the political account of that period, Dr Farooq Abdullah subsequently took him to the Nawai Subah party office and appointed him Provincial President to address his grievances.
History appears to have repeated itself.
Following the recent cabinet expansion, Gul was again taken to the National Conference headquarters at Nawai Subah, where Dr Farooq Abdullah and senior party leaders welcomed him with garlands.
An announcement was subsequently made appointing him General Secretary of the party.
Later the order was retracted.
Is this how National Conference appoints its office bearers?
This means all the elections held for different party posts in the past were just a mockery?
While an organisational position is important, it cannot automatically substitute for the responsibility and authority associated with a cabinet portfolio.
After nearly five decades of association with the party, Gul’s exclusion raises legitimate questions about how the NC rewards its veteran leaders.
Eidgah side-lined?
Mubarak Gul’s exclusion also brings into focus a wider question concerning the political representation and development of Eidgah constituency in Srinagar.
To my knowledge, no MLA representing Eidgah from 1947 till date has been appointed a minister, despite Gul’s repeated electoral victories.

This deserves closer examination, particularly when representatives from other constituencies in Srinagar and from relatively remote areas of Jammu and Kashmir have held ministerial positions or other significant responsibilities in different governments.
The issue is not merely about awarding a position to an individual politician.
It is also about whether the people of a constituency receive adequate political attention and effective representation within the government.
Eidgah has its own pressing civic and developmental concerns.
The Achan garbage dumping site, in particular, remains an important issue affecting residents and the surrounding environment.
Questions relating to waste management, public health, infrastructure and basic civic amenities require sustained political attention.
I believe that the perceived political marginalisation of Eidgah deserves serious scrutiny.

While the absence of a minister from a constituency does not, by itself, establish the cause of its developmental shortcomings, ensuring a stronger voice for the constituency in government could help its concerns receive greater attention.
The National Conference leadership should explain how it intends to address these longstanding grievances.
Pir Panjal and the question of regional representation.
The resentment expressed by Muzaffar Iqbal Khan highlights another important dimension of the cabinet expansion: the representation of the Pir Panjal region and the Pahari community.
Rajouri and Poonch occupy a strategically and politically significant position in Jammu and Kashmir.
Their people have distinct developmental priorities, including connectivity, healthcare, education, employment and access to public services.
The region also has a diverse social composition, making balanced political representation particularly important.

The disappointment expressed by MLAs from the region indicates that some elected representatives believe their constituencies have not received adequate consideration in the formation of the new Council of Ministers.
The Pahari community has several elected representatives, including leaders such as Dr Sajad Shafi, Javed Mirchal, Javed Hassan Beigh, Ajaz Jan and Muzaffar Iqbal Khan.
The precise number of MLAs belonging to the community and their respective constituencies should be established before drawing definitive conclusions about its representation.

In my assessment, the leadership should have considered inducting a minister from the Pahari community, particularly from Rajouri or Poonch, if the objective was to ensure a more equitable regional balance.
If the leadership considered retaining Shamima Firdous in the Council of Ministers, it could also have examined alternative arrangements for accommodating other regional aspirations.
Similarly, senior party leaders who were not inducted into the government could have been considered for important organisational responsibilities.
These are political choices, and reasonable people may disagree about the best combination of ministers.
However, a transparent explanation of the criteria used to select ministers would have helped address the resentment now visible within the party.
Abdul Majid Larmi, Dr Veeri.
The emotional reaction of Abdul Majid Larmi is another indication of the discontent generated by the cabinet expansion.
Larmi stated that he had been among the prospective candidates for ministerial induction and expressed dissatisfaction with the leadership’s decision concerning South Kashmir’s representation.
He also questioned the induction of Pahalgam MLA Altaf Kaloo, whom he considered junior to himself.

While seniority alone cannot be the deciding criterion for ministerial appointments, the disappointment of a three-time MLA deserves to be addressed through meaningful engagement rather than mere symbolic gestures.

Promising NC leaders like Dr Bashir Veeri have also been side-lined by the party, especially the CM who rebuked him on the floor of the house when he raised an issue related to the hike in electricity bills?
How can a CM behave like this with his MLAs?
Mir Saifullah deserved better consideration Apart from the selection of cabinet ministers, the allocation of portfolios also warrants closer examination.

Planning is an important department, and its significance should not be underestimated simply because Jammu and Kashmir is a Union Territory.
The division of powers between the elected government and the Lieutenant Governor does, however, affect the extent of the elected government’s authority in particular policy areas.
The real test is whether ministers are given portfolios that allow them to effectively use their experience and deliver tangible benefits to the people they represent.

Conclusion Omar Abdullah and the National Conference leadership must engage with their disgruntled legislators, address legitimate regional concerns and demonstrate that the government remains committed to serving every part of Jammu and Kashmir.
Let more Ministers be inducted in coming years by replacing the present Ministers.
Independent MLAs like Pyare Lal Sharma from Inderwal Kishtwar or Dr Rameshwar Singh from Banni Kathua can also be inducted in the cabinet in future to balance regional and religious aspirations.

stories.headline: One Health, One System
stories.title: One Health, One System
stories.summary: Many outbreaks that reach a hospital begin elsewhere, in wildlife or livestock, and cross into people through food, water or close contact. By the time the first case is diagnosed, the ecological event behind the outbreak may already be weeks old. That gap between the ecological event and the clinical diagnosis is the one that One Health, marked every year on November 3rd, is meant to close. The case for One Health rests on numbers that rarely change. The CDC and the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) estimate that about six in ten known human infectious diseases can spread between animals and humans, and roughly three in four new or emerging ones originate in animals. India is exposed by its own success. It is the world's largest milk producer and has one of the largest livestock populations, and its farms, forest fringes and informal markets bring people, animals and wildlife into constant contact. In such a landscape, the first sign of a human epidemic is often a pattern in animals that nobody connected: clustered abortions in cattle, unexplained deaths in a flock, a rise in fever cases at a primary health centre. Environmental change is steadily widening that exposure. Warmer, wetter conditions lengthen the breeding season and extend the range of insect vectors. Lumpy skin disease, caused by a capripoxvirus and spread by biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks, swept through Indian cattle in 2022 and has since reached many States, including Jammu and Kashmir. It does not infect people, yet it is a public health concern: it deprives households of milk, draught power and income, and these are the families least able to absorb the loss. Climate stress works through the food chain as well. Experimental work on elevated carbon dioxide has found lower nutrient composition in crops such as wheat and rice, while droughts and floods degrade fodder. Undernourished animals can be less productive and more susceptible to disease. More pests and fungi mean heavier pesticide use, and residues drain into rivers and aquatic food webs, returning the problem to human diets. Some risks reach us quietly, through the milk pail. Raw milk can carry bacteria such as Mycobacterium bovis, Brucella and Salmonella, which cause tuberculosis, brucellosis and salmonellosis in people. Brucellosis, for example, causes undulant fever, joint pain and fatigue, symptoms easily mistaken for typhoid or tuberculosis, so the disease is under-diagnosed and under-reported. Farmers and veterinarians carry occupational risk, and consumers carry the rest. Vaccinating female calves under the National Animal Disease Control Programme protects the herd, but it does not protect a household that receives unboiled milk from the unorganized sector. Pasteurization and the cold chain are therefore public health measures as much as dairy-economy ones. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is perhaps the clearest proof that the three domains are one. The Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance study in The Lancet estimated 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2021 and projected nearly 39 million cumulative attributable deaths between 2025 and 2050. Antibiotics given to animals for growth promotion, prophylaxis or unsupervised treatment select for resistant bacteria and resistance genes. These pass through manure, water, soil and food to people, and then back to animals. India banned colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, in food-producing animals in 2019, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has set residue limits. Enforcement, farm-level sales data and veterinary stewardship remain the weak links. The obstacle is institutional rather than scientific. Human disease surveillance sits with health authorities, animal disease reporting with animal husbandry departments, and wildlife and habitat data with forest and environment bodies. They rarely share a threshold for action, a database or a chain of command. Four global agencies, WHO, the Food and Agriculture Organization, WOAH and the UN Environment Programme, have drawn up a One Health Joint Plan of Action, but the real test is delivery in India’s districts. That begins with health, veterinary and environment teams meeting within hours of a suspected outbreak, guided by warning signs agreed in advance. It requires funded veterinary diagnostic laboratories linked to block-level dispensaries, with veterinarians treated as part of public health surveillance and not as a separate service. It requires a safer milk chain through pasteurisation and testing, antibiotics for animals sold only on prescription with sales recorded, and climate-linked surveillance of vectors and wildlife for early warning of outbreaks. Households can contribute too: boiling milk, cooking meat thoroughly, and washing produce are among the cheapest protections available. But the risk begins earlier, on the farm and in the environment. Protecting animals and the environment is part of protecting people. (The Author is a Veterinarian and an Independent Researcher. Email: dr.akhterrasool@rediffmail.com)

stories.headline: Jhelum is calling
stories.title: Jhelum is calling
stories.summary: River Jhelum, which is considered to be the lifeline of Kashmir, has been facing extreme ecological threat due to unabated pollution, illegal mining and encroachments. Jhelum serves a dual purpose for Kashmir—its major source for drinking water and irrigation and importantly saves the Valley from floods. Ironically the river has been fast losing both these functions in absence of conservation measures. Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir. The river is propelled by four streams—Sundran, Brang, Arapath and Lidder is Anantnag district. Besides small streams like Veshav and Rambiara also fed the river with fresh lease of waters. All water bodies flow into Jhelum making it an important part of Kashmir’s interconnected hydrological system. Despite its immense ecological importance, Jhelum is facing extreme pollution as all drains from south to north Kashmir directly flow into the river. The irony is that instead of constructing Sewage Treatment Plants, authorities have set up hundreds of pumping stations to empty drains into the river. The problem is compounded by dumping of solid waste and illegal sand mining. All these factors have severely affected flora and fauna and the hydrological system of the river. Jhelum has lost its carrying capacity also. It has been observed that the river swells and overflows after incessant rains for even 2-3 days. Wetlands like Hokersar, Bemina, Narakara, Batamaloo numbal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar and Gilsar on the left and right of Jhelum, which acted as reservoirs of floodwaters, have been encroached upon, filled and converted into colonies. Deterioration of these wetlands have affected their capacity to absorb flood water—putting extra pressure on Jhelum. Jhelum Action Plan formulated for four towns of Anantnag, Srinagar, Sopore and Baramulla to intercept, divert, transmit sewage of these areas and treat it in STPs is still on paper. The intervention of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir to restore the glory of Jhelum is timely. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney recently sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri, assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jhelum, raised concern over deteriorating condition of Jhelum. The Court has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody. It has also sought milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation. EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters. The PIL also highlights shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations. EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi minces no words to raise red flags over illegal mining, untreated sewage discharge and condition of river embankments saying this has significant implications for the river’s ecological health, carrying capacity and flood-management system. EPG rightly states that these concerns cannot be addressed through administrative assurances alone and require transparent information, scientific assessment and effective implementation on the ground. Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar. As per estimates flood water measuring about 120,000 cusecs surpassed the carrying capacity of Jhelum by five times. However no lessons have been learnt from the deluge. Despite the passage of 12 years, sustained and scientific measures are missing to increase the river’s carrying capacity. Believe it! Despite massive silt accumulation, no dredging has been undertaken in Jhelum in the last 5 years. On the other hand, unabated illegal mining in Jhelum’s tributaries —Doodh Ganga and Sukhnag has increased siltation in the river. An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years. This wanton extraction of riverbed material severely altered the natural course of the river and extensively damaged its flora and fauna. Besides, imagine how many tons of silt must have been deposited in river Jhelum. The Ram Bagh flood spill channel looks like a forest with heavy growth of grass and other vegetation. Near Tengpora bridge, a vast chunk of the flood spill has been converted into a football ground. When water level in Jhelum rises, these bottlenecks hamper free flow of water. It is shocking to see how habitations have come up in the Jhelum’s floodplains. It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods. Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas in central Kashmir Budgam areas. Now the Kandzal area is dotted with concrete constructions. The flood plains have been filled up! Earlier this year following incessant rains, Jhelum waters spread through its original flood plains from Shalina to Lasjan areas. The question is who allowed filling and constructions of Jhelum’s flood plains at the cost of endangering Srinagar city? Serious measures are missing to increase carrying capacity of Jhelum and restoration of its flood plains. We hope that judicial intervention will ensure long term conservation of Jhelum and restoration of its glory. And people shouldn’t forget that it’s also their responsibility to contribute their bit to protect their lifeline, the Jhelum. Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir.

sentences.text: Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar.
Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir.
An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years.
EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters.
